p.src: Now Xuande asked Kongming for a plan to resist Cao Cao’s army. Kongming said, “Xinye is a small county and cannot be held for long. I have lately heard that Liu Jingsheng is gravely ill. How could I bear to plot against him?” Kongming said, “If you do not take it now, regret will come too late.” Xuande said, “I would sooner die than commit an act that betrays righteousness.” Kongming said, “Then let us consider the matter further.”

p.src: Meanwhile, Xiahou Dun returned defeated to Xuchang, bound himself, appeared before Cao Cao, and prostrated himself to beg for death. Cao Cao pardoned him. Xiahou Dun said, “I fell victim to Zhuge Liang’s cunning scheme, and he routed my army with fire.” Cao Cao said, “You have commanded troops since youth. Did you not know that fire attacks must be guarded against in narrow places?” Xiahou Dun said, “Li Dian and Yu Jin did warn me of it, but regret now comes too late!” Cao Cao then rewarded the two men. Xiahou Dun said, “Liu Bei has grown so rampant that he is truly a mortal threat. He must be eliminated without delay.” Cao Cao said, “The only men who concern me are Liu Bei and Sun Quan. None of the others is worth my attention. Now is the time to sweep the southlands clean.” He thereupon ordered an army of five hundred thousand to be raised, appointing Cao Ren and Cao Hong to command the first division; Zhang Liao and Zhang He, the second; Xiahou Yuan and Xiahou Dun, the third; Yu Jin and Li Dian, the fourth; while Cao Cao himself led the other commanders as the fifth division. Each division commanded one hundred thousand troops. He further appointed Xu Chu General Who Breaks the Charge and gave him three thousand soldiers as the vanguard. The army was ordered to march on the bingwu day of the seventh month, in the autumn of the thirteenth year of Jian’an.

p.src: Kong Rong, Grand Master of the Palace, remonstrated: “Liu Bei and Liu Biao are both kinsmen of the imperial house and must not be attacked lightly. Sun Quan holds six commanderies like a crouching tiger and is protected by the natural barrier of the Great River; he too will not be easily overcome. If the Prime Minister now launches this unrighteous campaign, I fear he will forfeit the hopes of all under Heaven.” Cao Cao said angrily, “Liu Bei, Liu Biao, and Sun Quan are all ministers who defy imperial commands. How could they be left unpunished?” He drove Kong Rong away and decreed that anyone who remonstrated again would be beheaded. Leaving the residence, Kong Rong looked up to Heaven and sighed, “When consummate inhumanity attacks consummate benevolence, how can it avoid defeat?”

p.src: At the time, a retainer in the household of Imperial Censor-in-Chief Xi Lü heard these words and reported them to his master. Xi Lü had often suffered Kong Rong’s scorn and contempt and bore him a grudge, so he reported the words to Cao Cao; he added, “Kong Rong has habitually treated the Prime Minister with mocking disrespect, and he was also close to Mi Heng. Mi Heng praised Kong Rong by saying, ‘Confucius has not died.’ Kong Rong praised Mi Heng by saying, ‘Yan Hui has been born again.’ It was Kong Rong who prompted Mi Heng’s former humiliation of the Prime Minister.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and ordered the Commandant of Justice to arrest Kong Rong. Kong Rong had two young sons, who happened to be sitting opposite one another at home, playing a board game. Those around them hurriedly reported, “Your honored father has been seized by the Commandant of Justice and is about to be beheaded. Why do you two young masters not flee at once?” The two sons replied, “Beneath an overturned nest, how could any egg remain unbroken?”

p.src: While they were still speaking, someone reported that Cao Cao was personally leading a great army toward them. Xuande hurriedly took leave of Liu Biao and returned to Xinye through the night. When the ailing Liu Biao heard the news, he was greatly alarmed. He discussed drawing up a testament instructing Xuande to assist his eldest son, Liu Qi, as lord of Jingzhou. When Lady Cai heard of this, she was furious. She barred the inner gate and ordered Cai Mao and Zhang Yun to hold the outer gate. At the time, Liu Qi was in Jiangxia. Learning that his father was critically ill, he came to Jingzhou to visit him. As he reached the outer gate, Cai Mao barred his way and said, “Young lord, you were ordered by your father to guard Jiangxia, a duty of the utmost importance. Now you have abandoned your post without permission. What will you do if the forces of Eastern Wu arrive? If you enter to see our lord, he will certainly grow angry and his illness will worsen. That would be unfilial. You should return at once.”

p.src: Before the assembled officials could reply, the staff officer Li Gui answered, “Your words are most wise, young lord. You should immediately send a letter of mourning to Jiangxia and invite the eldest young lord to become lord of Jingzhou; at the same time, appoint Xuande to govern jointly with him. Then in the north you can withstand Cao Cao, and in the south resist Sun Quan. This is a plan that ensures complete security.” Cai Mao shouted, “Who are you to dare speak such reckless words in defiance of our lord’s dying command?” Li Gui cursed him loudly: “You have conspired within and without, falsely invoking our lord’s dying command, disinheriting the elder to enthrone the younger. Before our very eyes, you are delivering the nine commanderies of Jing and Xiang into the hands of the Cai clan! If our late lord’s spirit yet endures, he will surely strike you dead!” Cai Mao flew into a rage and ordered his attendants to drag Li Gui outside and behead him. Li Gui continued cursing until the moment of his death. Cai Mao then established Liu Cong as lord. Members of the Cai clan divided command of Jingzhou’s troops among themselves; Deng Yi, the Administrative Officer, and Liu Xian, the Aide-de-Camp, were ordered to guard Jingzhou. Lady Cai herself accompanied Liu Cong to garrison Xiangyang against Liu Qi and Liu Bei. Liu Biao’s coffin was buried on the Hanyang Plain east of Xiangyang, and neither Liu Qi nor Xuande was ever notified of his death.

Cao Cao now campaigns north and south in the name of the imperial court. If you resist him, my lord, your cause will lack legitimacy. Moreover, my lord, you have only just succeeded to your position; the threat from without is not yet quelled, and trouble within is about to arise. How could they oppose him?” Liu Cong said, “It is not that I refuse to follow your counsel. I merely fear that if I surrender my late father’s estate to another overnight, I shall become the laughingstock of the realm.”

p.src: Before he had finished, a man strode proudly forward and said, “Fu Gongti and Kuai Yidu have given excellent counsel. Why do you not follow it?” All looked and saw that he was Wang Can, courtesy name Zhongxuan, a native of Gaoping in Shanyang. Wang Can was slight and frail in appearance and short of stature; in his youth, he once went to visit the Court Gentleman Cai Yong. At the time Cai Yong’s hall was filled with eminent guests, yet on hearing that Wang Can had arrived, he hurried out to welcome him with his shoes reversed. The guests were all astonished and said, “Why does the Court Gentleman Cai show such singular respect to this mere boy?” Cai Yong replied, “This youth possesses extraordinary talent. I am no match for him.” Wang Can was widely learned and possessed a prodigious memory, beyond the reach of other men. Once, after reading a roadside inscription only once, he could recite it from memory; and after watching men play a game of go, when the stones were scattered, he restored the position without misplacing a single one. He was also skilled in calculation. His literary compositions were unrivaled in his age. At seventeen he was summoned to serve as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates, but declined the post. Later, fleeing disorder, he came to Jing and Xiang, where Liu Biao treated him as an honored guest.

p.src: Thus Liu Cong made up his mind, wrote a letter of surrender, and ordered Song Zhong to deliver it secretly to Cao Cao’s camp. Receiving his orders, Song Zhong went straight to Wancheng, gained an audience with Cao Cao, and presented the letter of surrender. Cao Cao was delighted and richly rewarded Song Zhong. He instructed Liu Cong to come out of the city to welcome him, promising that Liu Cong would remain lord of Jingzhou forever. Song Zhong took leave of Cao Cao and set out back toward Jing and Xiang. Just as he was about to cross the river, he suddenly saw a body of troops approaching. Looking closely, he saw that it was Guan Yunchang. Song Zhong could not evade him in time. Yunchang called him to a halt and questioned him closely about affairs in Jingzhou. At first Song Zhong concealed the truth, but unable to withstand Yunchang’s interrogation, he finally gave a full and truthful account of all that had happened. Yunchang was greatly alarmed. Yi Ji said, “If that is so, my lord, you should go to Xiangyang on the pretext of attending the funeral, entice Liu Cong to come out and welcome you, seize him on the spot, and execute his partisans. Jingzhou would then belong to you.”

p.src: Kongming said, “Jibo’s counsel is sound. My lord, you should follow it.” With tears falling, Xuande said, “At the point of death my elder brother entrusted his orphan to me. If I now seize his son and take his lands, when I die and descend to the Nine Springs, with what face could I meet my brother again?” Kongming said, “If you will not do this, Cao Cao’s troops have already reached Wancheng. How are we to resist them?” Xuande replied, “We had better withdraw to Fancheng and avoid them.”

p.src: While they were still deliberating, a scout galloped in to report that Cao Cao’s army had already reached Bowang. Xuande hurriedly sent Yi Ji back to Jiangxia to put the troops in readiness, while he himself consulted Kongming on a plan to resist the enemy. Kongming said, “Set your mind at ease, my lord. Last time, a single fire burned away more than half of Xiahou Dun’s army; now that Cao Cao’s army has come again, I shall certainly make them fall into this stratagem. We can remain in Xinye no longer. We had better go to Fancheng at once.” They had notices posted at all four gates, informing the inhabitants: “Whether old or young, man or woman, all who wish to follow us must come with us today to take temporary refuge in Fancheng. Do not bring calamity upon yourselves.” Sun Qian was sent to the riverside to requisition boats and assist the common people; Mi Zhu was sent to escort the families of the officers to Fancheng. Meanwhile, Kongming assembled the commanders to receive their orders. First he told Yunchang to take a thousand soldiers and lie in ambush upstream on the White River: “Each man is to carry sacks and fill them with sand and earth, damming the waters of the White River. After the third watch tomorrow night, when you hear men shouting and horses neighing downstream, quickly remove the sacks and release the water to drown them; then charge downstream with the current to support our forces.” Next he called Zhang Fei and ordered him to take a thousand soldiers and lie in ambush at the Boling ford: “The current is slowest here. Cao Cao’s troops, once flooded, will surely flee this way. Seize the opportunity to attack and support our forces.” Then he called Zhao Yun: “Take three thousand troops and divide them into four companies. Lead one company yourself and lie in ambush outside the eastern gate; deploy the other three outside the western, southern, and northern gates. First conceal large quantities of sulfur, saltpeter, and other combustibles on the roofs of houses within the city. When Cao Cao’s troops enter the city, they will certainly lodge in the people’s houses. After sunset tomorrow, a great wind is certain to rise. As soon as you see the wind rise, order all the troops concealed at the western, southern, and northern gates to shoot fire arrows into the city. Once the fire within the city is raging, raise a great clamor outside to swell our might. Leave only the eastern gate open for their escape, and you are to strike them from behind outside that gate. At daybreak, join forces with Generals Guan and Zhang, then withdraw the army to Fancheng.” He next ordered Mi Fang and Liu Feng to take two thousand troops, half bearing red banners and half green, and encamp before Quewei Slope, thirty li outside Xinye: “As soon as Cao Cao’s army appears, the red-banner troops are to flee to the left and the green-banner troops to the right. Suspecting a trap, they will surely not dare pursue you. You two are then to divide your forces and lie in ambush. When you see the fire rise in the city, pursue and slaughter the defeated troops; afterward, come upstream on the White River to support us.” When Kongming had completed all his dispositions, he climbed to high ground with Xuande to watch, awaiting only news of victory.

p.src: Now Cao Ren and Cao Hong led a hundred thousand troops as the vanguard, while Xu Chu went ahead with three thousand armored soldiers to clear the way. In a vast and imposing host, they swept toward Xinye. At around noon that day, they reached Quewei Slope and saw a body of troops before the slope, all displaying green and red banners. Xu Chu urged his troops forward. Liu Feng and Mi Fang divided their men into four companies, with the green and red banners withdrawing respectively to the left and right. Xu Chu reined in his horse and ordered, “Advance no farther. There must be an ambush ahead. Our troops will halt here.” Xu Chu galloped alone to report to Cao Ren in the vanguard. Cao Ren said, “This is a feint. There can be no ambush. Advance at once. I shall hurry the army forward behind you.”

p.src: Xu Chu returned to the foot of the slope and led his troops in an assault. But when they searched beneath the trees, not a single person was to be seen. By then the sun was sinking in the west. Just as Xu Chu was about to advance, a great din of drums and wind instruments arose on the mountain. Looking up, he saw a cluster of banners on the summit and two canopies amid them. Beneath the left sat Xuande and beneath the right Kongming, the two facing each other over wine. Xu Chu flew into a rage and led his troops in search of a path up the mountain. But rolling logs and hurled stones came crashing down from above, and he could advance no farther. Then tremendous battle cries arose behind the mountain. He wished to find a way through and engage the enemy, but night had already fallen.

p.src: Cao Ren arrived with his army and ordered that they first seize Xinye and rest their horses there. When the soldiers reached the walls, they found all four gates standing wide open. Cao’s troops rushed in without encountering any resistance. Not a soul could be found within the city either; it was nothing but an empty city.

p.src: Cao Hong said, “Outnumbered and out of stratagems, they must have fled with all the people. For now, let our army rest in the city. We shall advance at daybreak tomorrow.” By then every unit was weary from marching and the men were hungry, so they all went to find quarters and prepare their meals. Cao Ren and Cao Hong took their rest in the government offices. After the first watch began, a violent wind sprang up. The soldiers guarding the gates rushed in to report that a fire had broken out. Cao Ren said, “Some soldier must have been careless while cooking and let the fire spread. There is no cause for alarm.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, messengers came racing in one after another to report that fires had broken out at the western, southern, and northern gates alike. Cao Ren hastily ordered his officers to mount, but by then fires had erupted throughout the entire city, bathing everything from ground to sky in crimson light. p.src: Cao Ren led his officers through smoke and flame, desperately seeking an escape. Hearing that the eastern gate was untouched by fire, they hurried out through it. The soldiers trampled one another, and countless men died. Cao Ren and the others had only just escaped the fiery calamity when a battle cry arose behind them. Zhao Yun came charging up with his troops and plunged into the fight. The defeated soldiers fled for their lives; who among them would turn back to resist?

p.src: As they fled, Mi Fang arrived with another force. After another fierce charge, Cao Ren suffered a crushing defeat and forced a path of escape. Then Liu Feng appeared with yet another force and intercepted him for another attack. By the fourth watch, men and horses alike were exhausted, and more than half the soldiers had scorched hair and blistered faces. Reaching the bank of the White River, they were relieved to find the water none too deep, and men and horses alike entered the river to drink. The men shouted to one another, while all the horses neighed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Guan Yu had dammed the river upstream with sacks. At dusk he had seen Xinye go up in flames. At the fourth watch, hearing suddenly the shouts of men and neighing of horses downstream, he ordered his soldiers to pull away all the sacks at once. The released waters towered like the sky and surged downstream, drowning Cao’s men and horses; very many perished. Cao Ren led his officers toward a place where the current was gentler and fought his way to safety. When they reached the ferry at Boling, a tremendous battle cry arose. An army blocked their path, and at its head stood the great general Zhang Fei, who roared, “Cao’s villains, come quickly and surrender your lives!” Cao’s troops were greatly alarmed. Indeed:
